questions.q: Why does the lesson treat 'this is messy, we should clean it up' as not actually being a decision?
options: It expresses a feeling without computing the actual carrying cost of the debt or the break-even point of fixing it, so it provides no basis for deciding whether the fix is actually worth the cost
Messy code should always be left exactly as it is
Refactoring is always the correct choice regardless of any calculation
Code cleanliness has no real cost either way
questions.explain: A vague feeling that something is messy doesn't tell you whether fixing it is worth the engineering time -- that requires an actual cost comparison, same as Lesson 7's build-vs-buy framework.

questions.q: In the worked example, the refactor costs $3,600 upfront and saves $2,160/year in carrying cost, breaking even at 20 months. What does this number actually tell the team to ask next?
options: Whether this code is expected to still be in active use, receiving monthly changes, 20 months from now -- if it will be replaced sooner, the refactor never breaks even
Whether the refactor should be done immediately regardless of any other consideration
Whether the engineer who wrote the duplicated code should be reprimanded
The break-even number has no further implications once calculated
questions.explain: The break-even point only matters relative to how long the code will actually be around -- if it's replaced before 20 months pass, the refactor's cost is never recovered.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say code cleanliness and code LONGEVITY are different questions, and that the second one is what actually determines whether cleanup is worth it?
options: Even very messy code isn't worth refactoring if it will be retired before the refactor's cost is recovered, while even moderately messy long-lived code can be well worth fixing
Code longevity and cleanliness are always identical and can't be considered separately
Only code cleanliness matters -- longevity has no bearing on refactor decisions
Longevity is only relevant for code that's already been refactored once
questions.explain: A mid-level engineer often focuses only on 'this is messy'; the forward-looking question -- how long will this code realistically still be here -- is what the break-even math actually depends on.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is 'ship around it' (leaving the debt in place) the right call?
options: When the break-even math doesn't support paying it down given the code's real expected lifetime, or when something more urgent has a better return on the same engineering time right now
Ship around it is always the wrong choice regardless of circumstances
Ship around it is only acceptable if the code in question has zero bugs
Ship around it should be the automatic default whenever a refactor is even mentioned
questions.explain: The lesson frames 'ship around it' as sometimes the genuinely correct, reasoned decision -- not laziness -- when the economics or opportunity cost don't favor paying the debt down right now.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend capturing a 'ship around it' decision in an ADR or at minimum a comment, rather than leaving it as an implicit default?
options: A deliberate, reasoned decision to leave debt in place should be documented like any other architecture decision, rather than happening by default because no one ever explicitly decided anything
ADRs are only used for decisions to refactor, never for decisions to leave debt in place
Documenting this decision is purely a formality with no real value
This recommendation contradicts Lesson 6's guidance on ADRs
questions.explain: This connects back to Lesson 6 -- a conscious decision (even to defer action) deserves the same documented reasoning as any other architecture decision, so it doesn't read as an oversight later.
